---
title: "L23 & 24: two-sample t and paired t"
output: html_document
---

```{r load-libraries, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(RColorBrewer)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")
```

Every calculation from L23 and L24 in one runnable place. The lectures cover two new
flavors of t. The **two sample** test, for two independent groups, and the
**paired** test, for two measurements on the same units. Try the practice
problems at the bottom before checking the answers.

You need `weights.csv` in the same folder as this file.

## The three flavors of t

| Flavor | When to use it | R call |
|--------|----------------|--------|
| One sample | One group, compared to a fixed number | `t.test(x, mu = ...)` |
| Two sample | Two independent groups | `t.test(x, y)` |
| Paired | Two measures on the same units | `t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)` |

The two sample statistic replaces every piece of the one sample statistic:

$$t=\frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2)-(\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}$$

The key fact is in the denominator. For **independent** samples the variances
**add**, they do not subtract. Uncertainty never cancels.

# Part 1. Two independent samples

## Example: heights of US and Dutch born men

```{r heights-data}
set.seed(123)
dutch <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 183, sd = 7.4)
usa <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 175.5, sd = 7.4)

height_data <- data.frame(height = c(dutch, usa),
                          country = c(rep("Dutch", 100), rep("USA", 100)))

height_data %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(sample_mean = mean(height),
            sample_sd = sd(height),
            length = length(height))
```

Always plot before you test. Faceting gives one panel per group:

```{r heights-facet, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(height_data, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = country), binwidth = 5, col = "black") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  facet_wrap(~country, nrow = 2)
```

Without the facet the bars **stack**, so the y axis is the combined count of both
groups rather than the count in either one:

```{r heights-stacked, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(height_data, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = country), binwidth = 5, col = "black") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Box plots. Put the grouping variable on the x axis, otherwise the boxes land on a
meaningless numeric axis:

```{r heights-box}
ggplot(height_data, aes(x = country, y = height)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = country), col = "black") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

The test:

```{r heights-ttest}
t.test(usa, dutch, alternative = "two.sided")
```

The `data:` line of the output tells you which group R treated as x and which as
y, and therefore which way round the difference was computed. The sign of `t`
carries direction and nothing else.

## Example: transgenic chickens, worked by hand then checked

```{r chick-data}
transgenic <- c(38.8, 39.0, 39.7, 40.0, 40.8, 40.9, 41.0, 41.0, 41.0, 42.5,
                42.6, 43.0, 43.0, 43.4, 43.5, 43.5, 43.8, 44.4, 44.7, 44.7,
                44.7, 45.3, 45.7, 45.8, 46.4, 46.5, 46.6, 46.7, 46.7, 46.8,
                46.9, 47.1, 47.1, 47.1, 47.3, 47.6, 47.7, 48.1, 48.3, 49.3,
                49.3, 49.8, 50.3, 50.9, 52.1)

commercial <- c(36.7, 37.1, 38.9, 39.5, 39.5, 39.8, 40.0, 40.2, 40.3, 40.5,
                40.5, 40.7, 41.1, 41.2, 41.5, 41.5, 41.6, 41.6, 41.7, 42.4,
                43.1, 43.3, 43.3, 43.4, 43.7, 44.1, 44.2, 45.2, 45.3, 45.4,
                46.0, 46.1, 46.4, 46.6, 46.6, 46.9, 47.3, 47.5, 48.1, 48.2,
                48.4, 48.6, 49.0, 49.1, 49.3, 49.6, 50.1, 50.2, 50.4, 50.6,
                52.2, 53.0, 55.5, 56.4)

chicken_data <- data.frame(weight = c(transgenic, commercial),
                           type = c(rep("transgenic", 45),
                                    rep("commercial", 54)))
```

```{r chick-plots}
ggplot(chicken_data, aes(x = type, y = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = type)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

ggplot(chicken_data, aes(x = weight)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = type), binwidth = 3, col = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~type, nrow = 2) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Step 1, the estimate:

```{r chick-diff}
means <- chicken_data %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  summarise(mean_weight = mean(weight))

diff_means <- means[1, 2] - means[2, 2]   # commercial minus transgenic
diff_means
```

Step 2, the standard error:

```{r chick-se}
chicken_stats <- chicken_data %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  summarise(mean_weight = mean(weight),
            sd_weight = sd(weight),
            n = length(weight))
chicken_stats

se <- sqrt(4.568872^2/54 + 3.320836^2/45)
se
```

Step 3, the t statistic:

```{r chick-t}
t_stat <- (44.98889 - 45.14222 - 0)/se
t_stat
```

Now check against R. The degrees of freedom are not a whole number, because R
uses the Welch approximation:

```{r chick-ttest}
commercial_weight <- chicken_data %>% filter(type == "commercial") %>% pull(weight)
transgenic_weight <- chicken_data %>% filter(type == "transgenic") %>% pull(weight)

t.test(commercial_weight, transgenic_weight, alternative = "two.sided")
```

The p-value is 0.85, so there is no evidence the two groups differ. Note the
wording. We do **not** conclude the means are equal. The confidence interval adds
the useful part, any difference is almost certainly under 1.7 grams either way.

# Part 2. When the samples are NOT independent

```{r read-weights, message=FALSE}
weights <- read.csv(file = "weights.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
str(weights)
```

`weight1` is baseline weight, `weight3` is weight after 6 months in a weight loss
trial, and `dif2` is `weight3 - weight1`. All weights are in pounds.

## First, a genuinely independent comparison

Men versus women at baseline. These are different people, so a standard two
sample test is appropriate.

```{r sex-summary}
weights %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(sample_mean = mean(weight1),
            sample_sd = sd(weight1),
            length = length(weight1))
```

Two separate `geom_histogram` layers overlay rather than stack. The cost is that
you lose the automatic legend, so say which colour is which. Green is males, blue
is females:

```{r sex-hist}
ggplot(weights, aes(x = weight1)) +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(weights, sex == 'M'),
                 binwidth = 5, fill = "dark green", col = "green") +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(weights, sex == 'F'),
                 binwidth = 5, fill = "blue", col = "black") +
  labs(x = "Weight in pounds") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

The formula interface. Read `~` as "explained by", so outcome on the left and the
grouping variable on the right:

```{r sex-ttest}
t.test(weight1 ~ sex, data = weights, alternative = "two.sided")
```

## Now the same people, measured twice

Baseline against 6 months. These are the same 200 people, so the two columns are
linked row by row:

```{r wt-scatter}
plot(weights$weight1, weights$weight3,
     xlab = "Weight at baseline (pounds)",
     ylab = "Weight at 6 months (pounds)")

cor(weights$weight1, weights$weight3)
```

A correlation of 0.99 is the opposite of independence.

### The wrong test

Ignore the pairing and run the independent test anyway. The true effect built
into this simulated data is a 5 pound loss:

```{r wrong-test}
t.test(weights$weight1, weights$weight3)
```

The estimate is correct, about 5 pounds, but the p-value is 0.11 and the interval
contains zero. The 5 pound signal drowned in 30 pounds of between person noise.

### The right test

Look at the three standard deviations. This one table explains the whole lecture:

```{r paired-summary}
weights %>%
  summarise(dif_mean = mean(dif2), dif_sd = sd(dif2),
            wt1_mean = mean(weight1), wt1_sd = sd(weight1),
            wt3_mean = mean(weight3), wt3_sd = sd(weight3))
```

The **within** person standard deviation is about 4.85 pounds. The **between**
person standard deviations are about 30 pounds. The paired test uses the small
one.

```{r paired-test}
t.test(weights$weight1, weights$weight3, paired = TRUE)
```

Same data, same 5 pound estimate, p-value now below 0.0001. The only code change
was `paired = TRUE`.

Draw the two spreads on one axis to see why. Green is weight at 6 months, blue is
the within person difference:

```{r diff-hist}
ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(data = weights, aes(x = weight3),
                 binwidth = 5, fill = "green") +
  geom_histogram(data = weights, aes(x = dif2),
                 binwidth = 5, fill = "blue") +
  labs(x = "Weight in pounds") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

# Part 3. A small paired study, end to end

Eleven participants, cholesterol measured under each of two diets.

```{r chol-data}
set.seed(123)
trt_a <- c(155, 180, 190, 192, 203, 201, 207, 208, 217, 228, 237)

signal <- 7   # the true mean difference
noise <- 4    # 4/sqrt(11) = 1.21 is the true SE of the mean

trt_b <- trt_a + rnorm(length(trt_a), signal, noise)

chol_dat <- data.frame("A" = trt_a, "B" = trt_b, "id" = 1:length(trt_a))

chol_dat_long <- chol_dat %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(A, B), names_to = "diet", values_to = "cholesterol")
```

A plot that hides the pairing. The two clouds look the same:

```{r chol-jitter}
ggplot(chol_dat_long, aes(diet, cholesterol)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.03, pch = 21, size = 4, fill = "#2ca25f", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(y = "Cholesterol", x = "Diet") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

The independent test finds nothing:

```{r chol-indep}
t.test(x = chol_dat %>% pull(B),
       y = chol_dat %>% pull(A), mu = 0,
       alt = "two.sided", paired = FALSE, conf.level = 0.95)
```

Now connect each participant to themselves. Every single line goes up:

```{r chol-paired-plot}
means <- chol_dat_long %>%
  group_by(diet) %>%
  summarise(mean = round(mean(cholesterol), 1))

chol_dat_long <- chol_dat_long %>% mutate(diet_n = ifelse(diet == "A", 1, 2))
means <- means %>% mutate(diet_n = ifelse(diet == "A", 1, 2))

ggplot(chol_dat_long, aes(diet_n, cholesterol)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), lty = 3, lwd = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = as.factor(id)), pch = 21, size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Spectral") +
  labs(y = "Cholesterol", x = "Diet") +
  geom_text(data = means, aes(x = diet_n, y = 258,
                              label = paste0("Mean: ", mean)), size = 4) +
  expand_limits(y = 262) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend("ID")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), labels = c("A", "B"),
                     limits = c(0.5, 2.5)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank())
```

## The paired test by hand

The paired t test is a **one sample** t test on a single column of differences:

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_d - 0}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} \quad \text{on } n-1 \text{ degrees of freedom}$$

Step 1, collapse the pairs into differences:

```{r chol-diff}
chol_dat <- chol_dat %>% mutate(diff = B - A)
head(chol_dat)
```

Step 2, the estimate, its standard error, and t:

```{r chol-tstat}
summary_stats <- chol_dat %>%
  summarize(mean_diff = mean(diff),
            std_err_diff = sd(diff)/sqrt(n()),
            t_stat = mean_diff/std_err_diff)
summary_stats
```

Step 3, the p-value. `pt()` takes a value and returns a probability:

```{r chol-pval}
t_obs <- summary_stats %>% pull(t_stat)
pt(q = t_obs, lower.tail = FALSE, df = 10) * 2
```

Where that sits on the t distribution:

```{r chol-tplot}
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(-9, 9)), aes(x = x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 10)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-9, 9), breaks = c(-8, -4, 0, 4, 8)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_obs, t_obs), lty = 3) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dt, args = list(df = 10),
            fill = "blue", xlim = c(-9, -t_obs)) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dt, args = list(df = 10),
            fill = "blue", xlim = c(t_obs, 9)) +
  labs(x = "t distribution", y = "density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Step 4, the confidence interval. `qt()` takes a probability and returns a value:

```{r chol-ci}
q <- qt(p = 0.975, lower.tail = TRUE, df = 10)
q

mean_d <- summary_stats %>% pull(mean_diff)
se_d <- summary_stats %>% pull(std_err_diff)

c(mean_d - q * se_d, mean_d + q * se_d)
```

## The same thing in one line

```{r chol-paired}
paired_t <- t.test(chol_dat %>% pull(B), chol_dat %>% pull(A),
                   alternative = "two.sided", mu = 0, paired = TRUE)
paired_t
```

Independent versus paired on the identical 22 numbers:

| | Independent | Paired |
|---|---|---|
| t statistic | 0.78557 | 6.6033 |
| df | 19.976 | 10 |
| p-value | 0.4413 | 6.053e-05 |
| mean | 209.35 vs 201.64 | 7.72 |
| 95% CI | -12.78 to 28.21 | 5.11 to 10.32 |
| SE | 9.823 | 1.169 |

The estimate is identical. The standard error differs by a factor of 8, and that
one number drives everything else.

## Practice problems

**1.** Two independent groups. Group 1 has $n_1 = 30$, $\bar{x}_1 = 52$,
$s_1 = 9$. Group 2 has $n_2 = 25$, $\bar{x}_2 = 47$, $s_2 = 11$. Compute the
standard error of the difference and the t statistic.

```{r practice-1}
se_diff <- sqrt(9^2/30 + 11^2/25)
se_diff

t_prac <- (52 - 47 - 0)/se_diff
t_prac
```

Note the **plus** sign inside the square root. Variances add.

**2.** Using the conservative degrees of freedom, the smaller of $n_1-1$ and
$n_2-1$, get a two sided p-value for problem 1.

```{r practice-2}
2 * pt(q = abs(t_prac), df = min(30 - 1, 25 - 1), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

**3.** Ten patients have their blood pressure measured before and after a drug.
Which test do you use, and why?

Paired. The two columns describe the *same ten people*, so the measurements are
not independent. Compute each patient's change and run a one sample test on that
single column. Here is a worked version:

```{r practice-3}
set.seed(19)
before <- round(rnorm(10, mean = 145, sd = 15))
after <- before - round(rnorm(10, mean = 8, sd = 4))

bp <- data.frame(id = 1:10, before, after)
bp <- bp %>% mutate(change = after - before)
bp

t.test(bp$after, bp$before, paired = TRUE)
```

**4.** Rerun problem 3 as if the two columns were independent groups. What
happens to the p-value, and why?

```{r practice-4}
t.test(bp$after, bp$before, paired = FALSE)
```

The estimated difference is the same, but the standard error is built from
between person variation, which is much larger than the within person change. The
t statistic shrinks and the p-value grows. Compare the two standard deviations
directly:

```{r practice-4b}
bp %>% summarise(sd_change = sd(change),
                 sd_before = sd(before),
                 sd_after = sd(after))
```

**5.** You swap the arguments of `t.test` so the second group comes first. Which
parts of the output change?

The sign of `t`, the sign of the estimated difference, and the sign and order of
the confidence interval endpoints. The p-value and the degrees of freedom do not
change. Check it:

```{r practice-5}
t.test(bp$before, bp$after, paired = TRUE)
```

**6.** You have two samples of size 4 and 4 from populations with very different
shapes, one strongly skewed left and one strongly skewed right. Is a two sample
t test reasonable?

No. The t procedures tolerate $n_1 = n_2 = 5$ only when the two populations have
*similar* shapes. Opposite skewness is the worst case, because the skewness
reinforces instead of cancelling, and 4 observations per group is below even that
threshold.
